title: Past Events of Wulin
subtitle: Zhou Mi · Southern Song Lin'an · The Splendid Old Dream by West Lake
description: Zhou Mi (1232–1298), courtesy name Gongjin, sobriquet Caochuang, traced his ancestral home to Jinan but grew up in Lin'an (present-day Hangzhou). After the fall of the Southern Song, he lived in seclusion, refusing to serve the new dynasty. As a former subject, he recalled the lost splendor of the old capital Lin'an and wrote the ten-volume Past Events of Wulin around the twenty-seventh year of the Yuan Zhiyuan reign (1290). The book meticulously records the palaces, gardens, lakes, mountains, festivals, folk customs, cuisine, and arts of Southern Song Lin'an—a masterpiece that uses words to salvage the memory of a fallen nation. This route steps into Zhou Mi's Lin'an, seeking the lingering Southern Song spirit in present-day Hangzhou.

route.title: Past Events of Wulin: Zhou Mi's Southern Song Lin'an, the Broken Dream of the Old Capital by West Lake
route.intro:
West Lake is the finest scenery under heaven—at dawn and dusk, in rain and shine, every season holds its charms. And the people of Hangzhou are never without a reason to wander.
Zhou Mi was born into a family of officials—his great-grandfather was the famous Northern Song lyricist Zhou Bangyan, and his grandfather and father were both Southern Song officials. He grew up amid the lakes and mountains of Lin'an, spending his youth in the last decades of Southern Song splendor. On every festival, he would follow his family to watch the lanterns at West Lake, to burn incense at Lingyin Temple, to view the tidal bore on the Qiantang River—he knew Lin'an's delights intimately. In the second year of the Deyou reign (1276), the Yuan army captured Lin'an, and the Southern Song fell. Zhou Mi lost his city, and he lost his time. He lived in seclusion outside Hangzhou, spending the rest of his life writing a series of notebooks including Past Events of Wulin, Wild Words from the East of Qi, and Miscellaneous Observations from Guixin Street. The most moving of them all was this Past Events of Wulin, a remembrance of Lin'an's former splendor. He was not writing history—he was carving a "paper Lin'an" with every page steeped in longing for his lost country. Let us follow Zhou Mi's brush into that Lin'an which once made Marco Polo marvel and call it "the City of Heaven."

stops.title: Stop One: The Ten Views of West Lake—A Millennial Love Letter Between a Lake and a City
stops.content: Zhou Mi's description of West Lake in Past Events of Wulin is among the loveliest hymns to a lake in all Chinese prose. He wrote: "West Lake is the finest scenery under heaven—at dawn and dusk, in rain and shine, every season holds its charms." He loved everything about West Lake—the sparkling waves on sunny days, the misty haze in rain, the willows in spring, the moonlight in autumn. Past Events of Wulin records in detail every famous site around West Lake: Spring Dawn at Su Causeway, Lotus in the Breeze at Quyuan Garden, Autumn Moon over the Calm Lake, Snowy Remnants on Broken Bridge, Orioles Singing in the Willows, Fish Viewing at Flower Harbor, Thunder Peak Pagoda in Evening Glow, Twin Peaks Piercing the Clouds, Evening Bell at Nanping Hill, Three Pools Mirroring the Moon—this version of the "Ten Views of West Lake" was first codified by Zhou Mi and his literary friends in the Geographical Survey. From then on, the "Ten Views of West Lake" became the classic landscape picture in the Chinese imagination. Zhou Mi's West Lake was not only scenery but also people. He wrote: "The people of Hangzhou visit the lake mostly between noon and late afternoon." Painted pleasure boats crisscrossed the water, strings and woodwinds filled the air, flower sellers, singers, candied lotus-root vendors on the lake—the bustle of West Lake lives in these ordinary details. The third volume of Past Events of Wulin is devoted to boats on West Lake: "The large ones are called 'Great Green,' the next size 'Between Green,' and the smallest 'Little Green'"—Zhou Mi even distinguished the grades of boat names. He also recorded a special profession on the lake called "flower-selling grannies"—old women rowing small boats selling fresh blooms: "Flowers come in red and white, but only the white ones are most fragrant." These seemingly trivial records are what make Past Events of Wulin most moving—it is not about emperors and generals, but about those little people selling flowers by West Lake—because Zhou Mi knew that the true splendor of a city lies not in the grandeur of its palaces, but in the warmth of its streets. Zhou Mi also recorded an interesting incident: during the Chunxi reign, Emperor Xiaozong accompanied the Retired Emperor Zhao Gou on a lake tour—"the imperial boat had pearl curtains on all sides and embroidered sails and masts," and the people of the lake "all turned out to gaze upon it"—emperor and people enjoying West Lake together, a rare scene of peace. When Zhou Mi recalled this past in his later years, the Southern Song had already fallen. "Old travels are like a dream"—he summed up his years at West Lake in another notebook, Wild Words from the East of Qi. Most of the historical sites around West Lake are now Major Historical and Cultural Sites Protected at the National Level. The Wenlan Pavilion at the southern foot of Solitary Hill is a Qing-dynasty imperial library built to house the Complete Library of the Four Treasuries; its upturned eaves reflected in the lake make it a cultural landmark of West Lake. The Xiling Seal Society on Solitary Hill embodies a century of Chinese seal-carving art, with cliff inscriptions and pavilions scattered about, called "the finest spot on the lake and hills." And the Phoenix Temple on Zhongshan South Road—one of China's four great ancient mosques—bears witness to Southern Song Lin'an's openness as an international trading city. If Zhou Mi could revisit West Lake today, he would surely add a brilliant chapter to Past Events of Wulin for these new landmarks.

stops.title: Stop Two: Lingyin Temple—The Cold Spring Pavilion and the Peak That Flew Here
stops.content: Lingyin Temple is the oldest Buddhist monastery in Lin'an, founded in the first year of the Eastern Jin Xianhe reign (326) by the Indian monk Huili. By the Southern Song, it was nearly a thousand years old. In Past Events of Wulin, Zhou Mi devoted special attention to Lingyin Temple—especially the Peak That Flew Here (Feilaifeng) before the temple, with its "sheer cliffs and precipices, as if fallen from beyond the sky." The Feilaifeng Sculptures (including Southern Hill Sculptures) were carved continuously from the Five Dynasties through the Yuan dynasty, with over three hundred Buddhist figures distributed along the cliff faces by the stream. The most exquisite are the Yuan-dynasty Tibetan Buddhist-style images—the Ushnishavijaya, the Vajrapani, and others—whose lively postures and fusion of Han and Tibetan styles are unique in Chinese grotto art. The Lingyin Temple Stone Pagodas and Sutra Pillars—two Northern Song stone pagodas and two Five Dynasties sutra pillars—are masterpieces of Hangzhou Buddhist architecture. Zhou Mi's favorite spot was the Cold Spring Pavilion below Feilaifeng. He wrote: "The Cold Spring Pavilion stands below the Peak That Flew Here; the water murmurs, chilling to the bone." In summer, he and his friends would often bring wine and food to cool off here, watching the stream flow over the rocks—Southern Song summers were just that refreshing and pleasant. Lingyin Temple held a special place in Zhou Mi's heart—not only because of its antiquity, but because it was the root of Lin'an's Buddhism. Past Events of Wulin records that Lingyin Temple reached its peak scale in the Southern Song: "The temple had nine towers, eighteen pavilions, and seventy-two halls, with over 1,300 monk's quarters"—a single temple was a small city. Southern Song royalty and nobles frequently came to Lingyin Temple to offer incense, "with hundreds of attendants on horseback, incense smoke unbroken along the way." Zhou Mi himself preferred the quiet corners of the temple—the Cold Spring Pavilion below Feilaifeng was where he most often lingered. On the pavilion pillars was inscribed Bai Juyi's famous line: "When you reach the shore, please look back—Mount Penglai lies in the middle of the sea." Every time Zhou Mi read it, his heart ached with melancholy—Bai Letian's Hangzhou had long departed, and his Lin'an would also inevitably fade away. Throughout history, Lingyin Temple has been repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt. Its most recent large-scale restoration was in the Qing Kangxi reign—Emperor Kangxi, during his southern tour, inscribed the plaque "Chan Temple of Cloud Forest," which still hangs in the Mahavira Hall. The statue of Skanda in the Heavenly Kings Hall, carved from a single piece of camphor wood, dates from the Southern Song—it may have been the same Skanda that Zhou Mi gazed at when he paid homage. The seated Shakyamuni in the Mahavira Hall, 24.8 meters tall, was sculpted from twenty-four pieces of camphor wood joined together, created by teachers and students of the Zhejiang Academy of Fine Arts in 1953—China's largest indoor camphor-wood carved Buddha. Walking on Lingyin's stone paths, listening to the chanting from the Mahavira Hall, looking at the millennia-old smile on the cliffs of Feilaifeng—the Lin'an of Zhou Mi's pages never really went away.

stops.title: Stop Three: Jingci Temple and the Evening Bell at Nanping Hill
stops.content:
Jingci Temple, at the foot of Nanping Hill, was another major Southern Song Lin'an Buddhist stronghold. Past Events of Wulin records: "Jingci Temple is at the foot of Nanping Hill, built in the first year of the Zhou Xiande reign [954], originally named the Huiyong Yongming Monastery"—founded in the Later Zhou of the Five Dynasties, it had already enjoyed centuries of thriving incense by the Southern Song.

Jingci Temple is most famous for its "Evening Bell at Nanping Hill"—at dusk each day, the temple monks struck the great bell, its sound echoing through the valley, reaching every corner of West Lake. "Evening Bell at Nanping Hill" was one of the "Ten Views of West Lake" established by Zhou Mi and his literary friends. Its distant, ethereal resonance is among the most poignant scenes in classical Chinese aesthetics—the setting sun, the bell's lingering chime, the last golden-red light fading from the lake's surface: that was Zhou Mi's vision of the Southern Song's last twilight.

The temple's Jigong Hall enshrines the "Living Buddha Jigong" who became a monk at Jingci Temple in the Southern Song—a wild, eccentric yet miraculous legendary monk. In Past Events of Wulin, Zhou Mi mentions many of Lin'an's folk tales, and Jigong's story is the most vivid.

In the Southern Song, Jingci Temple's scale was second only to Lingyin Temple. Zhou Mi recorded in Past Events of Wulin the temple's Hall of Five Hundred Arhats—"the statues are exquisite, resplendent in gold and blue." Every New Year's Day, Lin'an's citizens, young and old, would come in throngs to burn the first incense at Jingci Temple—"the road before the temple streams with carriages and horses like flowing water, continuing until dusk." Jingci Temple and Thunder Peak Pagoda on the opposite shore of West Lake stood in perfect symmetry—"Thunder Peak is like an old monk, Baochu like a beauty." When the bell sounded, it was as if a layer of golden gauze spread across the lake.

On Sunset Hill opposite Jingci Temple, the Thunder Peak Pagoda collapsed with a thunderous roar in 1924, and was rebuilt on the original site in 2002—Zhou Mi's old scene of "Thunder Peak Pagoda in Evening Glow" has re-emerged. The gilded silver Ashoka pagoda and other precious artifacts unearthed from the pagoda's foundation confirm Zhou Mi's record that "this pagoda was built by Qian Hongchu, King of Wuyue, during the Five Dynasties." Jingci Temple and Thunder Peak Pagoda—one bell's sound, one pagoda's silhouette—have not left each other's side for a thousand years. Like Zhou Mi and his Past Events of Wulin: the man has departed, but that afternoon by West Lake will never vanish.

stops.title: Stop Four: Liuhe Pagoda—The Tide-Calming Treasure by the Qiantang River
stops.content: Past Events of Wulin mentions the Qiantang River many times—especially the great tidal bore every August. Zhou Mi wrote: "The tidal bore of Zhejiang is the grandest spectacle under heaven." He was the most seasoned observer of the Qiantang bore. During the Southern Song, on the eighteenth day of the eighth month each year, all of Lin'an would turn out to watch the tide at the riverbank—"carriages and horses block the roads; the prices of food and all goods double their usual." And the most striking structure on the Qiantang River's banks is the Liuhe Pagoda. Built in the third year of the Northern Song Kaibao reign (970), it was constructed by Qian Hongchu, King of Wuyue, in the hope that the Buddhist pagoda would tame the surging tide. The pagoda stands nearly sixty meters tall, octagonal, thirteen stories. Ascending to the top offers a magnificent view of the Qiantang River flowing into the sea. Zhou Mi often climbed Liuhe Pagoda—not to calm the tide, but to see far into the distance. From the pagoda, northward was West Lake, southward the Qiantang River, eastward the sea. In that moment at the pagoda's summit, all of Lin'an lay at his feet—the city he loved most, the city he spent his life guarding. In Past Events of Wulin, there is a classic passage about watching the Qiantang bore: Zhou Mi wrote that the bore first appeared "like a silver thread," then in a blink, "as it approached, it became a wall of jade and snow, stretching to the sky"—the rapid visual transformation from a fine silver thread to a sky-covering wall of snow, captured with exquisite precision. He also recorded the Southern Song court's "naval review" ceremony at the foot of Liuhe Pagoda: hundreds of warships maneuvering in formation on the river, "ten thousand sailors, shouts like thunder"—a military exercise that was also an annual national carnival. Since its completion in the Northern Song, Liuhe Pagoda has undergone many renovations. The current structure is a reconstruction from the twenty-sixth year of the Southern Song Shaoxing reign (1156), octagonal, thirteen stories, 59.89 meters tall. The brick-carved Buddha figures, flying apsaras, and floral motifs on its exterior are exquisitely refined—after more than eight hundred years of wind and rain, some details have blurred, but the solemn, flowing beauty has only deepened. Inside, a spiral staircase leads to the top; each level has murals of sutra illustrations and bodhisattva images—though later repainted, they retain an ancient charm. Across the river from Liuhe Pagoda stands the Qiantang River Bridge—the first dual-purpose road-rail bridge designed and built by Chinese engineers, by Mao Yisheng. Only eighty-nine days after its opening in 1937, to prevent the Japanese advance, Mao Yisheng personally demolished his own masterpiece. "Though the bridge died, its spirit did not"—this tragic heroism resonates deeply with the feelings of national loss that Zhou Mi expressed in Past Events of Wulin. Liuhe Pagoda has watched the Qiantang tide ebb and flow for a thousand years, and has watched the Chinese people journey from the grief of the Southern Song's fallen subjects to the confidence and composure of today.

stops.title: Stop Five: King Yue's Temple—The Verdant Hills Are Blessed to Bury the Loyal Bones
stops.content: Although Zhou Mi did not devote a special chapter to King Yue's Temple in Past Events of Wulin, he could hardly avoid it—for Yue Fei's tomb lay at the foot of Qixia Ridge by West Lake, separated from Lingyin Temple by only a single mountain. The Yue Fei Tomb was built after Emperor Xiaozong of the Southern Song posthumously rehabilitated Yue Fei. Before the tomb stands a stele reading "Tomb of Yue, Prince of E, Song Dynasty," as well as iron kneeling statues of the four treacherous ministers, including Qin Hui—"the verdant hills are blessed to bury the loyal bones, while white iron, though innocent, is cast into the images of traitors." As a Southern Song loyalist, Zhou Mi's feelings toward Yue Fei were deeply complex—on one hand, he revered the martyr's loyalty in resisting the Jin; on the other, he was filled with anguish—if Yue Fei had not died, perhaps the Southern Song would not have fallen. Every time Zhou Mi came to the foot of Qixia Ridge, he would stand long before Yue Fei's tomb. He lived in an era more tragic than Yue Fei's—Yue Fei died on the battlefield of the northern expedition; Zhou Mi lived in the ruins of a fallen nation. In Past Events of Wulin, he maintained a restrained sorrow—not weeping directly, but gently, over and over again, describing the Lin'an that could never return. The Yue Fei Tomb was first built in the thirty-second year of the Southern Song Shaoxing reign (1162)—upon ascending the throne, Emperor Xiaozong immediately rehabilitated Yue Fei, "restored his original rank, and reburied him with full honors" at the foot of Qixia Ridge. The cemetery covers about 15,000 square meters, with main buildings arranged along the central axis: the Temple of Loyalty, the Temple of Enlightenment, and Yue Fei's tomb. The stone figures and animals before the tomb—civil officials, generals, horses, rams, tigers—date from the Ming dynasty, their carving bold and powerful. The most eye-catching, and most infuriating, are the four iron kneeling statues beneath the tomb's gate tower—Qin Hui, Lady Wang, Moqi Xie, and Zhang Jun, hands bound behind their backs, kneeling forever. Since the Ming dynasty, countless visitors have cursed and beaten these iron figures, leaving dents in their iron chests. "The verdant hills are blessed to bury the loyal bones, while white iron, though innocent, is cast into the images of traitors"—this couplet before the tomb perfectly captures the Chinese people's most basic, most unwavering judgment of loyalty and treachery. After the fall of the Southern Song, Zhou Mi chose not to serve two dynasties—he lived in poverty for the rest of his life, but never set foot in the Yuan court. This same "loyalty" was cut from the same cloth as Yue Fei's "serve the country with utmost loyalty." The soughing pines on Qixia Ridge sounded like the warhorses of Yue Fei's northern expedition; the shimmering waters of West Lake below reflected the silent silhouette of a Southern Song loyalist. Zhou Mi did not write poems before Yue Fei's tomb—but the entire Past Events of Wulin, those gentle recollections of Lin'an's splendor, became the longest love letter of all to his fallen homeland.

stops.title: Stop Six: The Southern Song Lin'an City Site—The Lost Capital Buried Beneath Hangzhou
stops.content: The first volume of Past Events of Wulin describes the Southern Song imperial palace—the "Great Within." Zhou Mi meticulously recorded the palace's layout: the Lizheng Gate in the south, the Hening Gate in the north, and several dozen halls and pavilions within. "The palace chambers were built according to Lin'an's terrain, not following the old Central Plains conventions"—the Lin'an imperial palace was not as grand and orderly as Kaifeng's; instead, it adapted flexibly to the hills, carrying more of the charm of Jiangnan gardens. Yet this imperial palace, along with the entire Southern Song Lin'an city, is now mostly deeply buried beneath modern-day Hangzhou. After the Yuan destroyed the Song, Lin'an was systematically ruined—the imperial palace was turned into a Buddhist monastery and later destroyed by fire. Only scattered remains have been uncovered—a section of wall foundation, a few palace column bases, a stretch of blue stone from the Imperial Avenue—allowing us to touch that Lin'an of paper. In his old age, Zhou Mi lived in dire poverty, selling his writing to survive. But he never regretted spending his remaining years writing Past Events of Wulin. In his preface, he wrote: "Times have changed, circumstances have shifted, everything seems like another world." But he knew that as long as these words remained, Lin'an would never truly vanish. Whenever someone opens Past Events of Wulin, that city of heaven by West Lake comes alive on the page once more. Zhou Mi's record of Lin'an in Past Events of Wulin is astonishingly precise. When describing the layout of the "Great Within," he did not miss a single detail of the golden nails and vermilion doors. When writing of the "markets," he listed in detail the Pearl Market at Ronghe Ward, the Flower Market at Official Lane, the Medicine Market at Charcoal Bridge—these bits of seemingly trivial information have become vital evidence for archaeologists reconstructing Southern Song Lin'an. Since 1984, archaeologists have gradually uncovered the Southern Song Imperial Ancestral Temple site, the Imperial Avenue site, and the Deshou Palace site beneath Hangzhou, each excavation confirming Zhou Mi's records. The Lin'an City Site is the most precious cultural heritage beneath Hangzhou. The Imperial Ancestral Temple site revealed large-scale rammed earth platforms and column bases, proving that the Southern Song ancestral temple was far larger than documentary records suggest. The Imperial Avenue—present-day Zhongshan Road—has yielded multiple layers of road surfaces; the bottommost layer of Southern Song blue stone "fragrant cake bricks," neatly arranged, seems to still echo with the footsteps of officials heading to court eight hundred years ago. And the recently excavated Deshou Palace site—the retirement palace of Song emperor Gaozong—with its garden rockeries and pond remnants, confirms Zhou Mi's record that "the palace chambers were built according to Lin'an's terrain." Zhou Mi concluded the preface to Past Events of Wulin with the words: "Since I could not make a name in my own time, how could I hope to be remembered by posterity?"—he worried that no one would read his work. Eight hundred years later, his concern has clearly proved unfounded. Today, whenever a Southern Song site is excavated in Hangzhou, the first document archaeologists consult is Past Events of Wulin. That Lin'an of paper is slowly, piece by piece, emerging from beneath the ground back into the world of the living.
